items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Entrepreneurship might be the key to a longer life
items.content_html:
If you thought entrepreneurship was too stressful a path to venture down, you might want to reassess. A new study found that there may be a surprising benefit to starting a business: longevity. 

The study, titled “Do Entrepreneurs Live Longer?,” comes from researchers at the School of Business at Stevens Institute of Technology in New Jersey and was published in the Journal of Business on October 22. For the research, associate professor Cristiano Bellavitis and his collaborators examined 20 years of data from 27,501 Americans 50 and older.

Interestingly, it found that those who work for themselves may live longer than those who spend the bulk of their lives working for others: Entrepreneurs had a 10% lower risk of premature death. That was true even after researchers accounted for other factors that might tip the scale in either direction, such as age, income and wealth, and level of education.

The research offers a different perspective on work that can feel all-encompassing or lead to longer hours, which entrepreneurship is often associated with. While previous studies have found that long hours can lead to an uptick in death by heart-related illness, such as stroke, other considerations apparently come into play, such as the sense of freedom that can (sometimes) flow from working for yourself. 

Bellavitis said it’s a vital component that showed up in the study. “Most people think of entrepreneurship as extremely stressful, and it certainly can be. But entrepreneurship also gives people a high degree of autonomy and the opportunity to pursue something they genuinely love or care about,” he stated in a press release. “Our findings suggest those benefits may have lasting effects.”

Entrepreneurs are known to experience burnout in high numbers. However, the study revealed there was one major consideration that made the difference: The greatest advantage happened when that autonomy was the most present. “What seems to matter is not entrepreneurship alone, but the circumstances under which people enter it,” Bellavitis says. 

For example, when entrepreneurs launched businesses out of desire rather than necessity, longevity showed up. That means that, no matter what your profession—and whether you’re working for yourself or someone else—choice seems to matter deeply.

Longevity might be the biggest payout, but it wasn’t the only one the study spotted. Entrepreneurs reported lower levels of both depression and loneliness. While those are two mental health factors that can contribute to better health, they can also contribute to a greater sense of happiness. 

Therefore, entrepreneurship—at least when pursued out of passion and purpose rather than need—might not just be the key to a long life, but also a happy one.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication
items.content_html: Missing blood pressure medication could mean losing much of its protection against heart attacks and strokes, according to an analysis of more than 91,000 people. Patients who consistently took their medication experienced an 11% reduction in major cardiovascular events, while those who missed too many doses saw little or no measurable benefit.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
items.content_html: A major new study reveals that drinking just two alcoholic beverages a day is associated with a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of death from alcohol-related causes, challenging the idea that moderate drinking is harmless. Researchers also found no significant overall health benefits from alcohol, with risks rising as consumption increases.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
items.content_html: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
items.content_html: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and age-related damage.

items.title: [Nautilus] How Multiple Births Can Accelerate A Mother’s Biological Age
items.content_html:
As any mom can tell you, having a baby takes a big toll. Growing an entire new human being inside your body demands a lot of resources, energy, and time and it can lead to dramatic physiological changes. There’s some evidence that child-bearing benefits longevity, but pregnancy can accelerate biological aging as well. Now, a new review is trying to resolve this tension in the literature.   

Two geneticists from Harvard Medical School surveyed data gathered from studies that measured the biological age of women using a variety of methods, including wearable devices, blood tests and epigenetic clocks, and brain imaging. They found that pregnancy seems to speed up the biological clock, but it slows back down postpartum.  

Read more: “Pregnancy Changes Perception of Odors and Tastes”

items.title: [ArchDaily] Scaffolding as Interior Architecture: The Longevity of Temporary Structures
items.content_html: Scaffolding is perhaps one of architecture's most familiar temporary structures. It accompanies buildings through construction, maintenance, and renovation, only to disappear once its work is complete. Yet its apparent impermanence conceals a different kind of longevity. Scaffolding systems are designed to be assembled, dismantled, transported, and reused, with standardized components robust enough to withstand repeated handling and changing site conditions. Their temporary character lies less in the material itself than in the duration of each assembly.

items.title: [ft.com] Meta posts first free-cash-flow shortfall in at least a decade as AI spending climbs
items.content_html:
🎨 🏔️ ✏️

Meta reported $64.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 26% from a year earlier, but recorded its first quarterly free-cash-flow shortfall in at least a decade as it spent heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. The company also disclosed a new share arrangement for Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg, who had considered leaving California over a proposed billionaire wealth tax. Meta reported $9.9 billion in net income after recording a $9.9 billion charge tied to a settlement with U.S. states over claims involving teen mental health. The company spent about $35 billion on capital expenditures during the quarter and forecast spending as much as $145 billion in 2026. The new nonvoting Class C shares are intended to help Meta raise capital for AI investment and allow Zuckerberg to sell stock without surrendering voting control. He committed to remain in California, or wherever Meta is headquartered, for eight years. California voters decide the proposed wealth tax, Proposition 40, on Nov. 3, and Meta plans to issue the shares in January 2027.
